title: A MOTHER SAW WHAT COULD DESTROY HER SON BEFORE THE KINGDOM EVER FELL
paragraphs: A MOTHER SAW WHAT COULD DESTROY HER SON BEFORE THE KINGDOM EVER FELL

She warned him about women, wine, and the dangerous moment a man forgets who he belongs to. But hidden inside Proverbs 31:1–9 is a warning that reaches far beyond kings, exposes the battles we fight in secret, and points us toward the only King who never surrendered His righteousness.
“Give not thy strength unto women, nor thy ways to that which destroyeth kings.” — Proverbs 31:3 (KJV)
Imagine being powerful enough to command an entire kingdom… yet still being vulnerable to the very thing your mother warned you about when you were young.
Imagine having soldiers who would die for you, servants who would obey you, wealth beyond what ordinary people could dream of, and a throne that made men bow when you entered the room.
But somewhere behind the palace doors, there was a voice you could never completely silence.
Your mother's voice.
Not because she wanted to control you.
Not because she hated pleasure, distrusted every woman, or wanted you to live a miserable life.
But because she knew something that power has a terrible way of making people forget.
You can conquer a kingdom and still lose the battle for your own soul.
And perhaps the most frightening part of this story is that you do not need a crown to understand it.
You only need a weakness you keep defending.
A temptation you keep entertaining.
A habit you keep excusing.
A private compromise you keep promising God will be the last.
Because the ancient warning of Proverbs 31 was never meant to remain locked inside a palace.
It was meant to reach people like us.
People who love God but sometimes struggle to obey Him.
People who know Scripture but still wrestle with desire.
People who appear strong in public while quietly losing battles in private.
And people who have discovered, sometimes through devastating consequences, that the things we refuse to surrender to God can eventually begin to rule us.
The story begins with a mother speaking to her son.
“The words of king Lemuel, the prophecy that his mother taught him.” — Proverbs 31:1 (KJV)
The Hebrew introduces these teachings as divrei Lemuel melekh, massa asher yisserattu immo — the words of King Lemuel, an oracle or weighty message his mother taught him.

We are not told with certainty who Lemuel was. Some traditions have connected him with Solomon, but Scripture does not establish that identification. We should not turn speculation into biblical fact.
What Scripture does tell us is enough.
A mother was teaching a king how not to destroy himself.
And her first words are almost painfully tender.
“What, my son? and what, the son of my womb? and what, the son of my vows?” — Proverbs 31:2 (KJV)
In Hebrew, she repeatedly calls him beri — “my son.”
Then bar-bitni — “son of my womb.”
Then bar-nedarai — “son of my vows.”
Listen to the emotion in that repetition.
My son.
The child I carried.
The child connected to my deepest promises.
Before she addresses the king, she addresses the boy.
Before she speaks to his authority, she appeals to his identity.
Before she warns him about what he could lose, she reminds him that he was loved long before he ever wore a crown.
There is something almost unbearable about that.
Because mothers often remember what the world forgets.
The world sees the position.
A mother remembers the person.
The world applauds the achievement.
A mother remembers the tears.
The world sees a powerful man.
A mother remembers the child who once needed someone to hold his hand.
And now she must say something that could save him from becoming the very kind of ruler his people would one day fear.
“Give not thy strength unto women, nor thy ways to that which destroyeth kings.” — Proverbs 31:3 (KJV)
That verse can sound harsh when torn away from its context.
But we must be careful.
This is not a declaration that women are evil.
It is not permission for men to blame women for their own sinful choices.
It is not a condemnation of marriage, affection, or the God-given goodness of faithful love.
The Hebrew word translated “strength” is chayil, a word associated with strength, capability, valor, and resources.
The warning is about surrendering what God has entrusted to you to relationships or desires that lead toward ruin.
Notice the remarkable detail.
The same Hebrew word, chayil, appears later in Proverbs 31:10, where the excellent or virtuous woman is described as eshet chayil — a woman of strength, capability, and noble character.
The chapter that warns a king against destructive entanglements also celebrates the extraordinary worth of a godly woman.
That matters.
The problem is not womanhood. The problem is desire without wisdom, intimacy without faithfulness, and power without self-control.
A godly relationship can strengthen your calling.
An ungodly attachment can slowly consume it.
And sometimes destruction does not enter your life looking like destruction.
Sometimes it arrives looking like attention.
Like admiration.
Like a message you should not have answered.
Like someone who makes you feel understood when you have been emotionally neglected.
Like a relationship you insist is harmless, even while you begin hiding it from the people who trust you.
Sometimes the first thing temptation steals is not your marriage, your ministry, or your reputation.
It steals your honesty.
You begin deleting conversations.
Explaining away uncomfortable convictions.
Calling secrecy privacy.
Calling emotional dependency friendship.
Calling disobedience happiness.
And when your conscience becomes uncomfortable, you look for a way to quiet it instead of listening.
That is how compromise often works.
Not with one spectacular collapse.
But with small permissions.
One boundary crossed.
One warning ignored.
One lie justified.
One prayer postponed.
Until the person who once said, “I would never do that,” finds himself asking, “How did I get here?”
The Bible gives us a sobering example in Solomon.
Although we cannot establish that Solomon was Lemuel, his life illustrates the danger with heartbreaking clarity.
First Kings 11 tells us that Solomon loved many foreign women, including women from nations whose worship practices God had warned Israel against.
The issue was not their ethnicity. It was the spiritual allegiance and idolatrous influence involved in those unions.
Scripture says:
“For it came to pass, when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods: and his heart was not perfect with the LORD his God.” — 1 Kings 11:4 (KJV)
Read that slowly.
His heart was turned away.
This was the man associated with extraordinary wisdom.
The man who built the temple.
The man whose reign was marked by astonishing wealth and international influence.
Yet wisdom possessed is not always wisdom obeyed.
Knowledge of God is not the same thing as surrender to God.
You can explain temptation to someone else and still entertain it yourself.
You can quote Scripture while privately negotiating with sin.
You can lead others toward truth while allowing your own heart to drift away from it.
And the tragedy of Solomon's story is not simply that he made mistakes.
It is that the man who knew so much about wisdom did not consistently walk in the wisdom he knew.
Maybe that is what makes this passage uncomfortable.
Because some of us do not need another sermon telling us what is right.
We already know.
We know which relationship is crossing the line.
We know which habit is becoming a master.
We know which conversation should end.
We know which appetite is growing stronger every time we feed it.
We know the difference between conviction and condemnation, yet we sometimes use God's mercy as an excuse to postpone repentance.
And somewhere in the background, there may still be a voice warning us.
A parent.
A spouse.
A faithful friend.
A pastor.
Or the quiet conviction of Scripture that we keep trying to drown out.
Then the mother turns to another danger.

“It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine; nor for princes strong drink: Lest they drink, and forget the law, and pervert the judgment of any of the afflicted.” — Proverbs 31:4–5 (KJV)
Notice what she fears most.
She does not merely fear that her son might embarrass himself.
She fears that he might forget justice.
That he might become so clouded by indulgence that people who depend on his judgment would suffer.
The Hebrew word shikhar, translated “strong drink,” refers to an intoxicating beverage.
And the phrase translated “forget the law” carries the frightening idea of a ruler losing sight of the instruction or judgment he is responsible to uphold.

This passage is not a blanket statement that every use of wine is sinful. Scripture speaks about wine in more than one context, while repeatedly condemning drunkenness and warning against its destructive effects.
The immediate concern here is the king's responsibility.
A ruler cannot afford to surrender clear judgment when other people's lives depend on his decisions.
And that warning reaches much further than alcohol.
Because there are many ways to intoxicate the soul.
Some people drink to escape.
Some lose themselves in lust.
Some disappear into gambling, entertainment, endless scrolling, or compulsive spending.
Some become addicted to applause.
Some are intoxicated by power.
Some cannot tolerate silence because silence forces them to confront the pain they have been avoiding.
And some are not addicted to a substance at all.
They are addicted to being wanted.
To being admired.
To being right.
To having control.
To never feeling rejected again.
Not every coping behavior is an addiction, and not every struggle looks the same. But the spiritual question remains piercingly relevant.
What have you been turning to for relief that is slowly taking away your freedom?
Perhaps you are reading this late at night.
Everyone else is asleep.
The house is quiet.
Your phone is in your hand.
And you are exhausted from being the person everyone expects you to be.
You have responsibilities.
Bills.
People who need you.
Promises you are trying to keep.
You smile when necessary.
You answer, “I'm okay,” because explaining the truth feels too complicated.
But you know what happens when the loneliness becomes loud.
You reach for the thing that makes you forget.
Just for a while.
Just long enough to stop thinking.
Just long enough to stop feeling.
And afterward, the silence returns.
Except now it is carrying guilt.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe nobody suspects.
Maybe the people closest to you think you are stronger than you actually feel.
But God knows.
And this is where the Gospel becomes more than a religious idea.
Because Jesus Christ did not come merely to tell struggling people to try harder.
He came to save sinners.
He came to call people out of darkness.
He came to forgive what we could never erase by our own efforts.
And He came to give new life to people who have discovered that willpower alone cannot heal the deepest corruption of the human heart.
But before we rush toward comfort, we must hear the rest of this mother's warning.
Proverbs 31:6–7 says:
“Give strong drink unto him that is ready to perish, and wine unto those that be of heavy hearts. Let him drink, and forget his poverty, and remember his misery no more.”
These verses are sometimes misunderstood as an encouragement to escape life's pain through drunkenness.
But their setting is a contrast between a ruler's duty to maintain sound judgment and the desperate condition of those who are perishing or deeply distressed.
The passage reflects an ancient context in which intoxicating drink could be associated with relief for extreme suffering.
It should not be turned into a universal command to medicate emotional pain with alcohol.
And it certainly should not be used to justify self-destruction.
The mother is making a distinction.
The king has a responsibility that cannot be abandoned.
He must remain clear-minded because the vulnerable are depending on him.
Then she reveals the kind of king she wants her son to become.
“Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction. Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy.” — Proverbs 31:8–9 (KJV)
The word translated “dumb” in the King James Version means those who cannot speak or cannot effectively speak for themselves. It is not an insult.
The Hebrew command petach-pikha means “open your mouth.”
Speak.
Do not remain silent.
Use your authority to defend those who have little power.
Use your position to uphold righteousness.
Do not let your appetites consume the strength that was entrusted to you for the good of others.
Suddenly the passage becomes even more beautiful.
This mother was not simply raising a son who could avoid scandal.
She wanted a son who would protect people.
A king who would remember the forgotten.
A ruler whose power would not be spent entirely on himself.
And that exposes another uncomfortable truth.
Sometimes our private compromises are not as private as we imagine.
A father's unaddressed sin can wound his family.
A mother's secret dependency can affect those who rely on her.
A leader's dishonesty can injure an entire community.
A believer's refusal to repent can damage trust and obscure the beauty of the Gospel before watching eyes.
Our choices have consequences beyond ourselves.
Yet this is also where we must be careful not to confuse human weakness with hopelessness.
Because if Proverbs 31 shows us what a king ought to be, the rest of Scripture reveals the King who perfectly fulfilled righteousness.
Jesus Christ.
The King who was tempted, yet without sin.
The King who did not exploit the weak.
The King who defended the vulnerable.
The King who spoke truth when silence would have been easier.
The King who refused to exchange obedience to His Father for the kingdoms of this world.
When Satan offered Jesus worldly kingdoms in exchange for worship, Jesus answered with Scripture and refused. (Matthew 4:8–10)
Where earthly kings surrendered to temptation, Christ remained faithful.
Where rulers often protected their own comfort, Jesus gave Himself for others.
Where human power can become corrupted by self-interest, Jesus used His authority to serve.
And when He stood before Pontius Pilate, stripped of the outward appearance of earthly power, He was still the true King.
The One who would wear a crown of thorns before receiving the public recognition of His everlasting reign.
Think about the contrast.
A mother warned her son not to surrender his strength to what destroys kings.
But Jesus willingly laid down His life, not because temptation conquered Him, but because love moved Him to redeem sinners.
His surrender was not moral defeat.
It was perfect obedience.
His blood was not spilled because He lost control.
He gave His life willingly.
“No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself.” — John 10:18 (KJV)
And here is the part that should stop every weary, ashamed, struggling heart.
The King who never sinned was crucified for sinners.
The righteous One suffered for the unrighteous.
The innocent One bore the judgment our sins deserved.
Not because sin was harmless.
Not because holiness no longer mattered.
But because God's mercy is so profound that He provided, in Jesus Christ, the Savior we could never become for ourselves.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had repaired everything.
Not after our reputation was restored.
Not after we had conquered every temptation.
Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
That does not make repentance optional.
It makes repentance possible without despair.
The Greek word metanoeite, used in Jesus' call to repent in Mark 1:15, calls for a genuine turning of mind and life toward God.
Repentance is more than feeling terrible about what happened.
It is more than crying because consequences have arrived.
It is more than promising that next time will be different.
True repentance turns away from sin and toward God.
It stops defending what Christ died to forgive.
It begins telling the truth.
It accepts responsibility.
It seeks reconciliation where possible.
It takes practical steps to break patterns of disobedience.
And it rests not in personal perfection but in the mercy and power of Jesus Christ.
That means the man who has betrayed his marriage must not merely ask God to remove his guilt while continuing the betrayal.
He must turn away from the sin.
The person enslaved by alcohol or another destructive dependency may need honest confession, trusted support, and professional treatment alongside spiritual care.
The believer who has abused authority must not use forgiveness to escape accountability.
And the person who has been harmed by someone else's sin must never be pressured to pretend that repentance automatically restores trust or removes the need for safety and justice.
Grace does not erase the seriousness of evil.
Grace confronts evil with truth and offers redemption through Christ.
And sometimes the first evidence that grace is working in a person's heart is not a dramatic public testimony.
It is a quiet act of obedience.
An honest confession.
A deleted secret contact.
A decision to seek help.
A willingness to make restitution.
A difficult conversation.
A prayer whispered through tears.
“Lord, I cannot keep living like this.”
Perhaps that is where you are.
Not at the end of your faith.
But at the end of your excuses.
And maybe that is the beginning of something you have been praying for without realizing it.
Because the voice of Proverbs 31 is not merely asking, “What could destroy you?”
It is also asking, “What were you entrusted to protect?”
Your family?
Your integrity?
Your witness?
Your responsibilities?
The people who depend on your honesty?
The calling God has placed before you?
And most importantly, are you living as someone who belongs to Jesus Christ?
There is no need to pretend that every failure can be undone.
Some consequences remain.
Some relationships require years of rebuilding.
Some opportunities do not return.
Some wounds need time, accountability, and wise care.
But failure does not have to be the final word over the person who turns to Christ.
Consider Peter.
He denied Jesus three times.
He failed at the very moment he had confidently declared his loyalty.
And when the rooster crowed, Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Imagine the shame.
The memories.
The sound of his own voice denying the Lord he loved.
But the risen Jesus did not leave Peter forever defined by that terrible night.
In John 21, Jesus restored Peter to meaningful service, asking him about his love and entrusting him with care for His sheep.
Peter's denial was real.
His grief was real.
And Christ's restoring mercy was real.
That is the Gospel.
Not that scandal never happened.
Not that sin did not matter.
Not that broken trust can be repaired by a few religious words.
But that Jesus Christ can meet a repentant sinner in the ruins and begin a work of restoration that shame alone could never accomplish.
From scandal to grace does not mean the scandal was good. It means the grace of Jesus is greater than the sinner's power to save himself.
And perhaps the most moving detail of Proverbs 31 is that the mother never tells her son to become famous.
She does not tell him to accumulate more wealth.
She does not tell him to prove his greatness.
She tells him to guard his strength, preserve his judgment, and speak for those who cannot defend themselves.
In other words, do not waste your life on yourself.
And that is a warning our generation desperately needs.
We live in a world where attention is currency.
Where temptation is available through a screen.
Where private sin can be hidden behind a carefully curated image.
Where people may know how to build a following but not how to guard a conscience.
Where success can be measured in numbers while faithfulness quietly disappears.
But Jesus asks a far deeper question.
“For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?” — Mark 8:36 (KJV)
What good is the palace if the heart is in ruins?
What good is admiration if integrity is gone?
What good is influence if the people closest to you are suffering from the person you have become?
What good is religious language if you will not surrender to the Lord you claim to worship?
And what good is knowing the truth if you keep refusing to walk in it?
Maybe you were raised by a mother who prayed for you.
Maybe she warned you about people, habits, and choices that you did not understand at the time.
Maybe you dismissed her because you thought she was old-fashioned.
Maybe she is no longer alive, and you would give anything to hear her voice again.
Or maybe you never had a mother who spoke wisdom over your life.
Maybe your childhood was marked by neglect, confusion, or wounds that still ache.
Whatever your story, the truth of Scripture is not reserved for people who had perfect families.
God's Word is speaking to you now.
Not because you are a king.
But because your life matters.
Your decisions matter.
Your obedience matters.
And the people affected by your choices matter.
The Lord has not called you to live enslaved to every desire that demands your attention.
Through Christ, He calls you to walk in truth, holiness, love, and freedom.
And if you have fallen, His invitation is not to hide deeper in the darkness.
It is to come into the light.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Do you believe that?
Not merely as a verse for other people.
But for you.
For the secret you are ashamed to admit.
For the habit you have been fighting.
For the decisions you wish you could undo.
For the years you feel you wasted.
For the person you became while trying to fill a hunger that only God could ultimately satisfy.
Jesus does not offer permission to remain in bondage.
He offers forgiveness and new life.
And His grace is not exhausted by the depth of your need.
So tonight, or whenever these words find you, consider making one honest prayer.

“Lord Jesus, I have given too much of my strength to things that cannot save me. I have excused what You have called me to surrender. Forgive me. Teach me to love what is right. Give me courage to repent, wisdom to seek help where I need it, and a heart that belongs fully to You. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. I trust in Your mercy, not my own goodness. Lead me in Your truth. Amen.”
And if that prayer reflects the struggle of your heart, do not let this become another emotional moment that disappears when you close your phone.
Take the next faithful step.
Speak to someone trustworthy.
Open your Bible.
Return to prayer.
Seek accountability.
Make the decision you have been postponing.
Not to earn the love of God.
But because the love of God, received through Christ, calls us into a different way of living.
And if this message exposed something you have been hiding, I want to invite you into an honest conversation.
You do not have to reveal private details publicly. You can simply ask for prayer.
And if God has already brought you through a season of repentance and restoration, share a testimony of His faithfulness. Your words may encourage someone who believes change is impossible.
A father who is drifting.
A mother who is overwhelmed.
A young man who thinks temptation is harmless.
A young woman struggling to recognize her worth.
A believer who has grown cold.
A person who does not yet know Christ.
Someone who needs to discover that conviction can be an invitation to return to God rather than a sentence of hopelessness.
Not merely to increase its reach, but because Scripture deserves to be heard beyond the people who already agree with us.
There may come a day when the temptation you are resisting today returns with a different face.
And on that day, you may need to remember the mother's warning:
Do not give away the strength entrusted to you.
Do not surrender clear judgment to what clouds your mind.
Do not become so consumed by your own desires that you forget the people God has called you to love.
And above all, remember the King who gave Himself to save you.
This is why Gospel Warrior continues sharing Scripture-centered messages about repentance, forgiveness, discipleship, and the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
Because people need more than temporary inspiration.
They need the Word of God.
They need sound teaching.
They need encouragement grounded in biblical truth.
They need to know that following Christ is not simply about feeling moved by a message, but about learning to walk with Him day after day.
Scripture says in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Your generosity should come from a willing heart, not pressure or fear.
You glorify Him through faith in Christ, obedience, love, service, and faithful stewardship.
It can help us continue producing Christ-centered content, strengthen the ministry's reach, and pursue opportunities to serve more people with biblical encouragement and discipleship resources.
These are not simply items to collect. They can become useful reminders, meaningful gifts, and resources for encouraging conversations about faith.
Those free resources are part of our desire to make spiritual nourishment more accessible.
Keep reading.
Keep learning.
Keep growing in the Word.
And please keep sharing these messages with people who need to hear the Gospel.
Because the aim is not merely to build an audience.
It is to point people toward the Savior.
And before you leave, return with me to that palace one final time.
A mother is looking at her son.
Perhaps she sees the crown he will wear.
Perhaps she sees the temptations waiting beyond the palace walls.
Perhaps she knows that one day her voice will no longer be there to warn him.
So she gives him words she hopes he will carry for the rest of his life.
Guard your strength.
Guard your judgment.
Defend the vulnerable.
Remember who you are responsible to serve.
And thousands of years later, those words are still reaching hearts.
Including yours.
Maybe you cannot change yesterday.
Maybe you cannot recover every opportunity you lost.
Maybe the consequences of your choices are still painful.
But while you have breath, you can turn to Jesus Christ.
You can confess.
You can repent.
You can receive His forgiveness.
You can begin walking in the truth.
And you can trust that the risen Savior is able to continue His transforming work in the life of a person who comes to Him in faith.
The mother warned her son about the things that could destroy a king.
The Gospel reveals the King who came to rescue the people destroying themselves.
You may have given your strength to what was destroying you, but Jesus gave His life to redeem you.
